slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by contrasting this section with the preceding minimization lecture. For a convex minimum, local information can certify global optimality. For a convex maximum, the story moves to boundary geometry: faces, extreme points, and finite vertex checks when the feasible set is polyhedral.

slides.title: Maximum Versus Minimum
slides.notes: Emphasize the change in computational character. A convex function can have many local maxima on a convex feasible set, especially at sharp boundary points. After finding one local maximum, nearby comparisons do not tell us whether another face or vertex has a higher value.

slides.title: Interior Maximum Principle
slides.notes: The first theorem is the core warning. If a convex function reaches its supremum at a relative interior point of a convex set, the value cannot drop anywhere else in the set. The segment-through-the-interior argument turns any strict drop into a convexity contradiction.

slides.title: Maximizer Faces
slides.notes: Use this as a structural picture of all maximizers, not just one point. Each maximizer lies in the relative interior of a unique face. The interior maximum principle then forces the function to be constant on that whole face, so maximizers arrive in face-sized pieces.

slides.title: Convex Hull Reduction
slides.notes: Here the convex hull becomes a search-reduction tool. Since sublevel sets of a convex function are convex, controlling the function on the generating set controls it on the entire hull. Therefore the supremum over the hull is already visible on the generators.

slides.title: Boundary Reduction
slides.notes: This slide converts the hull theorem into a boundary principle. For many closed convex sets, the set is generated by its relative boundary, so a convex maximum does not need an interior search. The boundary is still large, but it is the first major dimension reduction.

slides.title: Extreme Point Principle
slides.notes: Now explain why vertices enter. Lineality directions carry constant values under the bounded-above hypothesis, and upward extreme directions cannot improve the value indefinitely. After quotienting out lines and pushing along rays, the supremum reduces to extreme points.

slides.title: Compact And Polyhedral Corollaries
slides.notes: This is the practical theorem students will remember. On a compact convex set inside the relative interior of the domain, continuity gives a finite attained maximum, and the preceding principle places some maximizer at an extreme point. For polyhedra, this becomes a finite vertex scan.

slides.title: Boundary Failures
slides.notes: The compact corollary has a real domain hypothesis. If the feasible set only sits in the domain and brushes a singular boundary, the supremum can be approached without being attained, or values can blow up. The examples in the source span are warning signs about boundary regularity.

slides.title: Subgradient Normal Certificate
slides.notes: Subgradients do not provide a global maximum test, but they still describe any attained nonconstant maximum in the relative interior of the domain. Every subgradient must be a nonzero outward normal to the feasible set, so the supporting linear function is also maximized there.

slides.title: Notebook Polygon Check
slides.notes: Tie the lecture back to the assigned notebook. The finite experiment samples a convex function on a polygon and verifies that the sampled grid values are bounded by the largest vertex value. It is not a proof of all theorems, but it is the executable invariant for this section.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close with a checklist. Convex maximization asks where the boundary, faces, and extreme points carry the high values. Interior maximizers imply constancy, convex hulls reduce the search, compactness gives attainment, and subgradients point normal to the feasible set at nonconstant maxima.
